items.stem: State what is meant by the term "action plan".
items.answer: A step-by-step schedule showing what will be done, when, and with which resources and sources
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a step-by-step schedule showing what will be done, when, and with which resources and sources. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why a research question should be focused rather than broad.
items.answer: A focused question (clear place, period, group) can be answered in depth with the time and sources available; a broad question leads to a shallow, descriptive answer.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A focused question (clear place, period, group) can be answered in depth with the time and sources available; a broad question leads to a shallow, descriptive answer. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "A research question must have a single correct answer." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Good I&S research questions are often open and allow a supported judgement rather than one fact.
items.markingKey: Good I&S research questions are often open and allow a supported judgement rather than one fact. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Which of the following is the most clear and focused research question for an investigation into formulating an inquiry question and an action plan?
options: Why did the population of Detroit fall between 1950 and 2020?
items.answer: Why did the population of Detroit fall between 1950 and 2020?
items.markingKey: A. It is open, has a clear scope (place/period/group) and can be answered with evidence; the others are too broad, closed or off-topic.

items.stem:
Source A – Student reflection (paraphrased): Reflection written by a Grade 8 student in an MYP I&S process journal, 2024

My first question was "What is climate change?" My teacher said it was too broad. I changed it to "How has the length of the dry season changed in Chennai since 1990?" Now I could find rainfall data from the Indian Meteorological Department and compare it with news reports.

Identify two points that Source A makes about formulating an inquiry question and an action plan, using evidence from the source.
items.answer: Narrowing the question made it possible to use specific data and sources.
items.markingKey: Narrowing the question made it possible to use specific data and sources. Award 1 mark per relevant point drawn from the source, up to [3]; own knowledge is not credited here. Criterion D: interpreting a source.

items.stem: You have three weeks to investigate "How effective were the Thames Barrier closures in protecting London from tidal flooding in the winter of 2013–14?" Outline a step-by-step plan, the sources you would use and one way you would evaluate your process at the end.
items.answer: Collect Environment Agency closure data; read news reports; compare tide levels with barrier closures; evaluate data reliability; present findings in a timeline and table.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Collect Environment Agency closure data; read news reports; compare tide levels with barrier closures; evaluate data reliability; present findings in a timeline and table. Credit: logical sequence of steps with a timeline; varied, appropriate sources (primary and secondary) named specifically; a method for recording and citing information (e.g. a source log in MLA/APA); a step for evaluating the process and results. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "open question"?
options: A note-taking method that divides the page into a notes column, a cue column of key questions and a summary
Descriptive information such as interviews, photographs or opinions
A question that cannot be answered with "yes" or "no" and invites explanation or evaluation
A step-by-step schedule showing what will be done, when, and with which resources and sources
items.answer: A question that cannot be answered with "yes" or "no" and invites explanation or evaluation
items.markingKey: C. "open question" is a question that cannot be answered with "yes" or "no" and invites explanation or evaluation.

items.stem: Distinguish between a research question and a topic.
items.answer: A topic is a broad area of interest (e.g. "migration"); a research question is a specific, open, answerable question within it (e.g. "Why did Syrian refugees settle in Gaziantep, Türkiye, between 2012 and 2016?").
items.markingKey: A topic is a broad area of interest (e.g. "migration"); a research question is a specific, open, answerable question within it (e.g. "Why did Syrian refugees settle in Gaziantep, Türkiye, between 2012 and 2016?"). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A survey of how students travel to school gave these results: walking 9, bicycle 22, bus 24, scooter 11. Calculate the percentage for each category and the angle each would have in a pie chart.
items.markingKey: Total = 66 (A1); % = value ÷ 66 × 100 (M1); angle = value ÷ 66 × 360 (M1); walking 13.6%, 49°; bicycle 33.3%, 120°; bus 36.4%, 131°; scooter 16.7%, 60° (A1, angles sum to 360°).

items.stem: "The research question is the most important part of an investigation." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: It is the foundation of a good investigation, but its value depends on being refined and supported by sound methods and analysis.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it sets the focus, scope and direction for all research; a weak question cannot be rescued by good research. Arguments against: good sources, methods and analysis are equally necessary; questions are often refined during the investigation. Supported judgement: It is the foundation of a good investigation, but its value depends on being refined and supported by sound methods and analysis. Markbands (12 marks): MYP I&S criterion D (year 3), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly analyses concepts and issues, summarises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, analyses a range of sources in terms of origin and purpose recognising value and limitations, and clearly recognises different perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2 limited, mostly assertion.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Putting someone else's ideas into your own words, while still citing the source"?
items.answer: paraphrase
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of paraphrase.

items.stem: "If you change a few words, you do not need to cite the source." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Ideas taken from a source must be cited even when paraphrased; changing words does not make them your own.
items.markingKey: Ideas taken from a source must be cited even when paraphrased; changing words does not make them your own. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why it is useful to collect both quantitative and qualitative data.
items.answer: Numbers show patterns and size (how much, how many), while interviews and observations explain reasons and experiences, giving a fuller answer. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Numbers show patterns and size (how much, how many), while interviews and observations explain reasons and experiences, giving a fuller answer. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Source A – School academic integrity policy (paraphrased): Summary of a typical IB school academic integrity policy, based on IB "Academic integrity" guidance (2019)

Students must acknowledge all sources used in their work, including words, ideas, images, data and AI-generated content. Work submitted must be the student's own. Failure to cite sources is treated as academic misconduct, even if it was not intended.

With reference to its origin and purpose, analyse the value and limitations of Source A for a student investigating collecting and recording information: note-taking and citing sources.
items.answer: Origin: Summary of a typical IB school academic integrity policy, based on IB "Academic integrity" guidance (2019). Purpose: to set rules for students and explain the consequences of misconduct. Value: It reflects IB expectations and shows how seriously schools treat citation. Limitation: It is a policy, so it states rules rather than explaining how to cite in practice.
items.markingKey: Origin: Summary of a typical IB school academic integrity policy, based on IB "Academic integrity" guidance (2019). Purpose: to set rules for students and explain the consequences of misconduct. Value: It reflects IB expectations and shows how seriously schools treat citation. Limitation: It is a policy, so it states rules rather than explaining how to cite in practice. Award up to [3]: origin and purpose identified and USED (not just copied), at least one value and one limitation explicitly linked to them. Reliability is judged for a purpose, not as "biased = useless". MYP I&S criterion D (year 3), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly analyses concepts and issues, summarises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, analyses a range of sources in terms of origin and purpose recognising value and limitations, and clearly recognises different perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2 limited, mostly assertion.

items.stem: A survey of how students travel to school gave these results: scooter 22, bicycle 26, bus 16, car 8. Calculate the percentage for each category and the angle each would have in a pie chart.
items.markingKey: Total = 72 (A1); % = value ÷ 72 × 100 (M1); angle = value ÷ 72 × 360 (M1); scooter 30.6%, 110°; bicycle 36.1%, 130°; bus 22.2%, 80°; car 11.1%, 40° (A1, angles sum to 360°).

items.stem:
Source A – School academic integrity policy (paraphrased): Summary of a typical IB school academic integrity policy, based on IB "Academic integrity" guidance (2019)

Students must acknowledge all sources used in their work, including words, ideas, images, data and AI-generated content. Work submitted must be the student's own. Failure to cite sources is treated as academic misconduct, even if it was not intended.

Identify two points that Source A makes about collecting and recording information: note-taking and citing sources, using evidence from the source.
items.answer: All sources, including AI tools, must be acknowledged; not citing is misconduct.
items.markingKey: All sources, including AI tools, must be acknowledged; not citing is misconduct. Award 1 mark per relevant point drawn from the source, up to [3]; own knowledge is not credited here. Criterion D: interpreting a source.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Using the internet makes research easier but less reliable."
items.answer: The internet makes research easier and can be reliable if students check origin, purpose and corroborate information.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: information is quick to find and up to date; many reliable sources (UN, government data) are online. Arguments against: much online content is unverified, biased or out of date; students may copy rather than evaluate. Supported judgement: The internet makes research easier and can be reliable if students check origin, purpose and corroborate information.

items.stem: Evaluate the research question "Do students plagiarise?" for an MYP Individuals and Societies investigation into collecting and recording information: note-taking and citing sources. Rewrite it so that it is clear, focused and researchable.
items.answer: Weakness: it is a closed and accusatory question that would be hard to answer honestly Improved: "How do students at our school choose and record sources when researching for I&S assignments?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it is a closed and accusatory question that would be hard to answer honestly); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "How do students at our school choose and record sources when researching for I&S assignments?" (clear scope – place, period or group – and open, researchable wording); 1 mark: justification of the change. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Briefly explain why it is useful to collect both quantitative and qualitative data.
items.answer: Numbers show patterns and size (how much, how many), while interviews and observations explain reasons and experiences, giving a fuller answer.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Numbers show patterns and size (how much, how many), while interviews and observations explain reasons and experiences, giving a fuller answer. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between a quotation and a paraphrase.
items.answer: A quotation uses the author's exact words in quotation marks; a paraphrase restates the ideas in your own words. Both must be cited.
items.markingKey: A quotation uses the author's exact words in quotation marks; a paraphrase restates the ideas in your own words. Both must be cited. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Tariq argues that "Using the internet makes research easier but less reliable." Lars disagrees. Explain one piece of evidence each student could use, and state which view you find more convincing and why.
items.answer: The internet makes research easier and can be reliable if students check origin, purpose and corroborate information.
items.markingKey: Tariq: information is quick to find and up to date. Lars: much online content is unverified, biased or out of date. Judgement (1-2 marks): The internet makes research easier and can be reliable if students check origin, purpose and corroborate information.

Students must acknowledge all sources used in their work, including words, ideas, images, data and AI-generated content. Work submitted must be the student's own. Failure to cite sources is treated as academic misconduct, even if it was not intended.

Using Source A and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim that "Using the internet makes research easier but less reliable."

items.markingKey: From the source: All sources, including AI tools, must be acknowledged; not citing is misconduct. items.stem: Which question tests the purpose of a source?
items.answer: Why was it made, and for whom?
items.markingKey: Why was it made, and for whom?. Purpose concerns motive and audience.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a source can be valuable even if it is unreliable about events.
items.answer: It can reveal the beliefs, attitudes and propaganda methods of its creator and audience – e.g. a wartime poster shows how governments tried to influence people.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It can reveal the beliefs, attitudes and propaganda methods of its creator and audience – e.g. a wartime poster shows how governments tried to influence people. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Government statistics are always completely reliable." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: They are often reliable but can be affected by how data are collected, political pressure or definitions; they should still be evaluated.
items.markingKey: They are often reliable but can be affected by how data are collected, political pressure or definitions; they should still be evaluated. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe the 1858 Punch cartoon "Father Thames Introducing His Offspring to the Fair City of London" and explain what it reveals about evaluating visual sources.
items.answer: Published during the "Great Stink", it showed the polluted river as an old man presenting diseases such as cholera and diphtheria as his children to London. A satirical cartoon exaggerates but reveals public concern that pushed Parliament to fund Bazalgette's sewers.
items.markingKey: Context (Published during the "Great Stink", it showed the polluted river as an old man presenting diseases such as cholera and diphtheria as his children to London.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: a satirical cartoon exaggerates but reveals public concern that pushed Parliament to fund Bazalgette's sewers. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to evaluating visual sources.

items.stem: Using accurate subject terminology and at least one specific example, write a structured paragraph that responds to: Explain why the purpose of a source affects its reliability.
items.answer: A source made to persuade, sell or justify may select facts or exaggerate, so its account may be one-sided; a source made for private record may be more candid.
items.markingKey: Content: A source made to persuade, sell or justify may select facts or exaggerate, so its account may be one-sided; a source made for private record may be more candid. Structure: a clear point that answers the question, specific evidence, explanation that links evidence to the point, and a closing link. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Write the introduction and an outline of the body paragraphs for an essay that evaluates the view that "Primary sources are more useful than secondary sources for an MYP investigation."
items.answer: Thesis: Neither is automatically more useful: usefulness depends on the question, and strong investigations combine both.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they give direct evidence and original perspectives; they let students do their own analysis. Counter-arguments: secondary sources provide context and summarise many primary sources; primary sources may be biased, incomplete or hard to interpret. Thesis/conclusion: Neither is automatically more useful: usefulness depends on the question, and strong investigations combine both. Credit a thesis that answers the question, logically ordered paragraphs each with specific evidence, a counter-argument that is weighed, and a conclusion that follows. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: A source written 200 years after an event by a historian is…
items.answer: a secondary source
items.markingKey: D. The historian was not present.

items.stem: A class brainstorm on evaluating sources by their origin, purpose and reliability produced the question "Is the news fake?" Explain why it needs refining, then suggest an improved research question and justify your change.
items.answer: Weakness: it is a broad, closed question with no defined sources or event Improved: "How reliable are online news reports about a recent local flood, and how do they compare with official data?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it is a broad, closed question with no defined sources or event); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "How reliable are online news reports about a recent local flood, and how do they compare with official data?" (clear scope – place, period or group – and open, researchable wording); 1 mark: justification of the change. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Describe the research methods you would use to answer "How reliable are online news reports about a recent local flood, and how do they compare with official data?", naming specific sources and explaining why each is appropriate.
items.answer: Collect five news reports and the official Environment Agency (or national) report; analyse each with OPVL; compare facts in a table; identify bias; write conclusions; cite sources.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Collect five news reports and the official Environment Agency (or national) report; analyse each with OPVL; compare facts in a table; identify bias; write conclusions; cite sources. Credit: logical sequence of steps with a timeline; varied, appropriate sources (primary and secondary) named specifically; a method for recording and citing information (e.g. a source log in MLA/APA); a step for evaluating the process and results. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Which of these is an annotation rather than a label?
options: "Steep slope – fast runoff increases flood risk"
items.answer: "Steep slope – fast runoff increases flood risk"
items.markingKey: C. An annotation explains.

items.stem: Sana writes: "A long answer is always a better answer." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Quality depends on focus, structure, evidence and explanation; extra words without analysis add nothing.
items.markingKey: Quality depends on focus, structure, evidence and explanation; extra words without analysis add nothing. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between a description and an explanation.
items.answer: A description says what something is like or what happened; an explanation gives reasons why or how it happened.
items.markingKey: A description says what something is like or what happened; an explanation gives reasons why or how it happened. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using accurate subject terminology and at least one specific example, write a structured paragraph that responds to: Explain why the audience should affect how findings are communicated.
items.answer: Different audiences need different vocabulary, detail and formats – a report for a council needs data and recommendations, a poster for students needs clear visuals and simple text.
items.markingKey: Content: Different audiences need different vocabulary, detail and formats – a report for a council needs data and recommendations, a poster for students needs clear visuals and simple text. Structure: a clear point that answers the question, specific evidence, explanation that links evidence to the point, and a closing link. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Justify the relevance of the research question "How can we best present the results of our traffic survey to persuade the city council to install a pedestrian crossing?"
items.answer: It links communication (criterion C) to a real audience and purpose.
items.markingKey: It links communication (criterion C) to a real audience and purpose. Award marks for relevance to the unit's concepts or global context, and for showing the question is focused and can be answered with available sources. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem:
Source A – Report extract (paraphrased): Paraphrase of Florence Nightingale, "Notes on Matters Affecting the Health, Efficiency and Hospital Administration of the British Army", 1858

The author showed with a diagram that, in the first winter of the war, deaths from preventable diseases in army hospitals were many times greater than deaths from battle wounds. She argued that better sanitation, ventilation and food would save thousands of soldiers' lives.

Using Source A and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim that "Visual presentations communicate findings better than written reports."
items.answer: Each has strengths: the most effective communication combines clear visuals with written explanation suited to the audience.
items.markingKey: From the source: Most soldiers died from preventable disease, so hospital sanitation must improve. Own knowledge for: graphs and maps show patterns quickly and memorably; they make data accessible to wider audiences. Own knowledge against: written reports can explain causes, nuance and limitations; visuals can mislead if poorly designed. Judgement: Each has strengths: the most effective communication combines clear visuals with written explanation suited to the audience. Top answers integrate the source with own knowledge and comment on the source's origin/purpose. MYP I&S criterion D (year 3), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly analyses concepts and issues, summarises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, analyses a range of sources in terms of origin and purpose recognising value and limitations, and clearly recognises different perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2 limited, mostly assertion.

items.stem: Explain why the structure of a response matters to the reader.
items.answer: A clear structure – introduction, logically ordered paragraphs and conclusion – lets the reader follow the argument and see how evidence supports each point.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A clear structure – introduction, logically ordered paragraphs and conclusion – lets the reader follow the argument and see how evidence supports each point. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Which of these is the correct APA (7th edition) reference for Tim Marshall's book "Prisoners of Geography: Ten Maps That Tell You Everything You Need to Know About Global Politics" (Elliott and Thompson, 2015)?
options: Tim Marshall. Prisoners of Geography: Ten Maps That Tell You Everything You Need to Know About Global Politics. Elliott and Thompson, 2015.

items.markingKey: C. APA: Author surname, initials (year). Title in sentence case. Publisher.

items.stem: Plan an extended response to the question: "Visual presentations communicate findings better than written reports." To what extent do you agree? Give a thesis, two arguments with specific evidence, a counter-argument and a conclusion.
items.answer: Thesis: Each has strengths: the most effective communication combines clear visuals with written explanation suited to the audience.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: graphs and maps show patterns quickly and memorably; they make data accessible to wider audiences. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "bibliography".
items.answer: An alphabetical list of all the sources used in an investigation, written in a recognised format such as MLA or APA
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: an alphabetical list of all the sources used in an investigation, written in a recognised format such as MLA or APA. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A testable statement that predicts the answer to a research question"?
items.answer: hypothesis
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of hypothesis.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Why the source was made and who it was made for"?
items.answer: purpose
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of purpose.

items.stem: Suggest and justify the most appropriate graph or map to present data on the movement of migrants from five countries to Germany. State two features your graph must include.
items.answer: A flow-line map – arrow width shows the size of each flow between places
items.markingKey: A flow-line map (1); justification: arrow width shows the size of each flow between places (1); features (1): title, labelled axes with units or key, scale, source of data. Criterion C ii.

items.stem: Distinguish between quantitative data and qualitative data.
items.answer: Quantitative data are numerical (counts, measurements); qualitative data are descriptive (interviews, photos, opinions).
items.markingKey: Quantitative data are numerical (counts, measurements); qualitative data are descriptive (interviews, photos, opinions). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between bias and perspective.
items.answer: Perspective is the viewpoint every source has; bias is when that viewpoint leads to a one-sided or distorted account.
items.markingKey: Perspective is the viewpoint every source has; bias is when that viewpoint leads to a one-sided or distorted account. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Suggest and justify the most appropriate graph or map to present data on monthly temperature and rainfall in Mumbai. State two features your graph must include.
items.answer: A climate graph (bars for rainfall, line for temperature) – it combines two variables measured monthly
items.markingKey: A climate graph (bars for rainfall, line for temperature) (1); justification: it combines two variables measured monthly (1); features (1): title, labelled axes with units or key, scale, source of data. Criterion C ii.

items.stem: Explain why a source log saves time at the end of an investigation.
items.answer: Recording author, title, date, publisher or URL as you go means the bibliography can be built quickly and accurately, with no lost sources.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Recording author, title, date, publisher or URL as you go means the bibliography can be built quickly and accurately, with no lost sources. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Using accurate subject terminology and at least one specific example, write a structured paragraph that responds to: Explain why an action plan helps an investigation succeed.
items.answer: It breaks the task into steps with deadlines, identifies sources early, and lets the student check progress and adjust before running out of time.

items.stem: You have three weeks to investigate "How can we best present the results of our traffic survey to persuade the city council to install a pedestrian crossing?" Outline a step-by-step plan, the sources you would use and one way you would evaluate your process at the end.
items.answer: Analyse traffic count data; choose appropriate graphs; draft a one-page report and a poster; ask three adults for feedback; revise; evaluate which format persuaded best.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Analyse traffic count data; choose appropriate graphs; draft a one-page report and a poster; ask three adults for feedback; revise; evaluate which format persuaded best. items.stem: Which of these is the correct APA (7th edition) reference for Peter Frankopan's book "The Silk Roads: A New History of the World" (Bloomsbury, 2015)?

items.stem: Explain why "How has the number of street trees in our neighbourhood changed between 2015 and 2025?" is a suitable research question for an MYP investigation into formulating an inquiry question and an action plan.

items.stem: Explain why "How reliable are online news reports about a recent local flood, and how do they compare with official data?" is a suitable research question for an MYP investigation into evaluating sources by their origin, purpose and reliability.
items.answer: It applies source evaluation (criterion D) to a real local event with sources that can be compared.
items.markingKey: It applies source evaluation (criterion D) to a real local event with sources that can be compared. items.stem:

The author showed with a diagram that, in the first winter of the war, deaths from preventable diseases in army hospitals were many times greater than deaths from battle wounds. She argued that better sanitation, ventilation and food would save thousands of soldiers' lives.

Explain one value and one limitation of Source A for an investigation into communicating findings in structured paragraphs, maps and graphs, referring to its origin and purpose.
items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of Florence Nightingale, "Notes on Matters Affecting the Health, Efficiency and Hospital Administration of the British Army", 1858. Limitation: It was written to campaign for reform, so the data were selected and presented to persuade.

items.stem: Formulate an action plan to investigate the research question "How do students at our school choose and record sources when researching for I&S assignments?" Include the main steps, at least one primary and one secondary source, and how you would record your findings.
items.answer: Design an anonymous survey; collect 40 responses; examine five sample bibliographies (with permission); calculate percentages; present findings; evaluate honesty of responses.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Design an anonymous survey; collect 40 responses; examine five sample bibliographies (with permission); calculate percentages; present findings; evaluate honesty of responses. items.stem:
Source A – Student reflection (paraphrased): Reflection written by a Grade 8 student in an MYP I&S process journal, 2024

My first question was "What is climate change?" My teacher said it was too broad. I changed it to "How has the length of the dry season changed in Chennai since 1990?" Now I could find rainfall data from the Indian Meteorological Department and compare it with news reports.

Using Source A and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim that "The research question is the most important part of an investigation."
items.answer: It is the foundation of a good investigation, but its value depends on being refined and supported by sound methods and analysis.
items.markingKey: From the source: Narrowing the question made it possible to use specific data and sources. Own knowledge for: it sets the focus, scope and direction for all research; a weak question cannot be rescued by good research. Own knowledge against: good sources, methods and analysis are equally necessary; questions are often refined during the investigation. Judgement: It is the foundation of a good investigation, but its value depends on being refined and supported by sound methods and analysis. Top answers integrate the source with own knowledge and comment on the source's origin/purpose. items.stem:

items.answer: Neither is automatically more useful: usefulness depends on the question, and strong investigations combine both.

items.stem: A class brainstorm on communicating findings in structured paragraphs, maps and graphs produced the question "What is a graph?" Explain why it needs refining, then suggest an improved research question and justify your change.
items.answer: Weakness: it is a definition question with nothing to investigate Improved: "How can we best present the results of our traffic survey to persuade the city council to install a pedestrian crossing?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it is a definition question with nothing to investigate); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "How can we best present the results of our traffic survey to persuade the city council to install a pedestrian crossing?" (clear scope – place, period or group – and open, researchable wording); 1 mark: justification of the change. items.stem: Which of these is a primary source for a study of your town's traffic?
items.answer: Your own traffic count
items.markingKey: B. You collected it first-hand.

items.stem: Which of these is the best research question for an MYP investigation?
options: "How did the 2015 earthquake affect tourism in Kathmandu between 2015 and 2018?"
items.answer: "How did the 2015 earthquake affect tourism in Kathmandu between 2015 and 2018?"
items.markingKey: A. It is open, focused on a place, period and impact, and researchable.

items.stem: Define the term "limitation".
items.answer: What reduces a source's usefulness or reliability for a particular question
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: what reduces a source's usefulness or reliability for a particular question. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why the audience should affect how findings are communicated.
items.answer: Different audiences need different vocabulary, detail and formats – a report for a council needs data and recommendations, a poster for students needs clear visuals and simple text.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Different audiences need different vocabulary, detail and formats – a report for a council needs data and recommendations, a poster for students needs clear visuals and simple text. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "A bibliography only needs to list books." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: It must include every source used – websites, interviews, videos, maps and data sets as well as books.
items.markingKey: It must include every source used – websites, interviews, videos, maps and data sets as well as books. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why an action plan helps an investigation succeed.
items.answer: It breaks the task into steps with deadlines, identifies sources early, and lets the student check progress and adjust before running out of time.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It breaks the task into steps with deadlines, identifies sources early, and lets the student check progress and adjust before running out of time. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between perspective and bias.
items.answer: Perspective is the viewpoint every source has; bias is when that viewpoint leads to a one-sided or distorted account.
items.markingKey: Perspective is the viewpoint every source has; bias is when that viewpoint leads to a one-sided or distorted account. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "A long answer is always a better answer." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Quality depends on focus, structure, evidence and explanation; extra words without analysis add nothing.
items.markingKey: Quality depends on focus, structure, evidence and explanation; extra words without analysis add nothing. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between qualitative data and quantitative data.
items.answer: Quantitative data are numerical (counts, measurements); qualitative data are descriptive (interviews, photos, opinions).
items.markingKey: Quantitative data are numerical (counts, measurements); qualitative data are descriptive (interviews, photos, opinions). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student wants to survey 24 of the 600 households on a housing estate using systematic sampling. What sampling interval should be used, and how would the sample be chosen?
items.answer: Every 25th person
items.markingKey: Interval = population ÷ sample = 600 ÷ 24 = 25 (M1); start at a random number from 1 to 25, then select every 25th (A1).

items.stem: Using Charles Minard's map of Napoleon's Russian campaign (1869) as an example, explain combining data on a map.
items.answer: A single flow map shows the size of the army, its route, the temperature and dates, as the army shrank from about 422 000 to about 10 000 men. One well-designed graphic can show several variables and tell a clear story.
items.markingKey: Context (A single flow map shows the size of the army, its route, the temperature and dates, as the army shrank from about 422 000 to about 10 000 men.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Write the introduction and an outline of the body paragraphs for an essay that evaluates the view that "Using the internet makes research easier but less reliable."
items.answer: Thesis: The internet makes research easier and can be reliable if students check origin, purpose and corroborate information.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: information is quick to find and up to date; many reliable sources (UN, government data) are online. Counter-arguments: much online content is unverified, biased or out of date; students may copy rather than evaluate. Thesis/conclusion: The internet makes research easier and can be reliable if students check origin, purpose and corroborate information. Credit a thesis that answers the question, logically ordered paragraphs each with specific evidence, a counter-argument that is weighed, and a conclusion that follows. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: "Visual presentations communicate findings better than written reports." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Each has strengths: the most effective communication combines clear visuals with written explanation suited to the audience.
